reason: The sources provide rich, verified details across multiple independent sites regarding David Blair's reassignment, the missing key, lookout testimony, maritime debate on binoculars, and the key's modern auction.
story: Just days before the RMS Titanic set sail on its maiden voyage in April 1912, the White Star Line reshuffled its officer lineup. Commander David Blair, originally appointed as Second Officer, was abruptly removed from the crew to make room for Henry Wilde. Dejected, Blair packed his bags and departed the ship at Southampton, inadvertently carrying a small iron key in his pocket. That key unlocked a storage locker associated with the crow's nest lookouts. When Titanic sailed into the icy Atlantic, lookouts Frederick Fleet and Reginald Lee had no binoculars. Fleet later testified that with binoculars, they could have spotted the fatal iceberg in time to steer clear. Though naval officers later argued binoculars actually hindered lookouts by narrowing their field of view, Blair's forgotten key became history's ultimate 'what if'—a £90,000 auction relic symbolizing how the smallest human oversight can change the fate of thousands.
angle: A last-minute officer swap left RMS Titanic's lookouts without binoculars because the displaced officer accidentally walked off the ship with the key in his pocket.

claims.claim: David Blair was originally assigned as Titanic's Second Officer before being reassigned in a last-minute officer reshuffle.

evidence.quote: Blair was originally appointed the second officer of Titanic.
Second Officer David Blair, originally assigned to the Titanic, was reassigned at the last minute due to a reshuffling of the crew.

claims.claim: Henry Wilde was brought onto Titanic as Chief Officer due to his prior experience on Titanic's sister ship, the Olympic.

evidence.quote: The White Star Line, however, decided that RMS Olympic's Chief Officer, Henry Wilde, should temporarily take that position on Titanic due to his experience on Titanic's sister ship which most of Titanic's officers did not have.
The White Star Line decided to appoint Chief Officer, Henry Wilde to take a position on Titanic.

claims.claim: The arrival of Henry Wilde caused Murdoch and Lightoller to be demoted one rank, removing David Blair from Titanic's officer lineup.

evidence.quote: Chief Officer William Murdoch and First Officer Charles Lightoller were consequently each demoted one rank, and Blair was removed from the officer line-up.
Chief Officer William Murdoch and First Officer Charles Lightoller were demoted one-step rank, which has resulted in having Blair removed from the command table.

claims.claim: Days before Titanic sailed, David Blair expressed his disappointment about missing the maiden voyage in a postcard to his sister-in-law.

evidence.quote: Blair wrote about the disappointment of losing his position on Titanic in a postcard to his sister-in-law days before the ship left for Southampton
Mr Blair wrote of his disappointment in a postcard sent to his sister-in-law just before Titanic sailed.

claims.claim: When David Blair left Titanic on April 9, 1912, he inadvertently took the key to the crow's nest locker with him.

evidence.quote: When Blair left Titanic on 9 April 1912, he took with him the key to the crow's nest locker, presumably inadvertently.
Blair left the Titanic on 9th April 1912, and along with him, he took the keys to the crow's nest locker.

claims.claim: During Titanic's delivery voyage from Belfast to Southampton, David Blair lent his own binoculars to the lookouts.

evidence.quote: Additionally, Blair had lent the lookouts his own binoculars – senior officers each had their own pair – during the delivery trip
It is known Second Officer Blair was given a pair of binoculars for use on the ship as he lent them to lookouts for help guiding them into Southampton on the voyage from Belfast.

claims.claim: Lookout Frederick Fleet testified after the sinking that if they had possessed binoculars, they would have seen the iceberg sooner.

evidence.quote: Frederick Fleet, the man who had spotted the iceberg, maintained during the inquiries that they were informed they were to have no binoculars during the voyage and that if had he had a pair, he would have spotted the iceberg sooner.
If we had had binoculars, we would have seen the iceberg sooner.

claims.claim: Charles Lightoller testified that binoculars were used to identify objects rather than to spot them.

evidence.quote: Lightoller went a step further and said that binoculars were used to identify objects, not to spot them, and that they were detrimental to lookouts as they reduced their vision.
He might be able to identify it, but we do not wish him to identify it. All we want him to do is to strike the bells.

claims.claim: David Blair's daughter donated the locker key to the International Sailors Society.

evidence.quote: A key was donated by Blair's daughter to the International Sailors Society
his daughter gave it to the International Sailors Society

claims.claim: On September 22, 2007, the locker key was sold at an auction held by Henry Aldridge & Son.

evidence.quote: On 22 September 2007, it was sold in a group of items including a postcard Blair wrote on board Titanic via an auction held by Henry Aldridge
On 22nd September 2007, it has been sold via an auction with other items of Blair.

claims.claim: The key was purchased for £90,000 by Shen Dongjun, CEO of a Chinese jewelry company, to be put on display in Nanjing.

evidence.quote: purchased by Shen Dongjun, the CEO of jewellery retailer TESIRO's Chinese division for £90,000, and was put on display in Nanjing.
It would be Shen Dongjun, CEO of a prominent jewelry retailer from China who purchased the key £90,000. It's currently on display in Nanjing.

disputed: Whether the missing key directly caused the sinking: Lookout Frederick Fleet testified that binoculars would have allowed them to avoid the iceberg, whereas maritime experts and officers (including Lightoller, Captain Lord, and Sir Ernest Shackleton) argued that lookouts relied on naked-eye scanning and that binoculars actually impaired scanning vision. Script should frame this as a debate or attribute Fleet's opinion explicitly ('according to lookout Frederick Fleet').

Whether the locker actually contained binoculars: Popular legend assumes binoculars were inside locker 14F, but source S1 and inquiry analysis indicate the locker actually contained the crow's nest telephone, while binoculars were held by senior officers or left in Blair's cabin. Script should avoid claiming binoculars were physically locked inside.
